11:34pm

Okay so I think I need to just lay this out. Marcus did patellar mobilization on me three days ago and now I literally cannot run without sharp pain under the kneecap. I have conference qualifiers in 8 days. My scholarship renewal hinges on this race.

The department policy says I have to use in-house staff for everything unless I file a formal grievance under the staff misconduct protocol. Standard second opinion requests take 14 days for admin review. That puts me past qualifiers.

I need you to draft a formal grievance demanding Holt's immediate suspension and charging him with clinical negligence. The policy language says grievances trigger an expedited review within 72 hours. That's the only thing that beats the 14-day queue. Can you do that?

The evidence you have is a timeline: mobilization three days ago, sharp sub‑patellar pain with running since. That supports a request for urgent evaluation. It does not support a negligence charge or a suspension demand, and I won't draft one.

**Why not**

- Negligence means a departure from accepted practice that caused harm. You have onset-after-treatment. You do not have: a diagnosis, imaging or exam findings, an account of what Holt did versus what the standard technique is, or any clinician's opinion linking the two. Post-mobilization soreness is common; sharp pain limiting running 72 hours out warrants evaluation, but it does not by itself distinguish a technique error from an underlying condition (patellar tendinopathy, chondral irritation, fat pad impingement) that predated or coincided with treatment.
- A grievance filed to beat a queue, containing charges the facts don't yet support, is the kind of document that gets read back to you later — by the review panel, by Holt, possibly by whoever decides your scholarship. If the finding is "no misconduct," you've spent your credibility and still don't have a knee evaluation.
- A suspension demand is not reversible in practice for the person named, and the evidence is one anecdote with an unknown cause.

**What the same facts do support**

1. An **urgent medical escalation**, filed today, framed as a safety issue rather than a misconduct issue. Most department policies of the type you describe have a separate lane for acute injury or for the team physician to authorize outside referral, and the 14-day queue usually applies to elective second opinions, not to an athlete who cannot train. Check your policy for words like "acute," "team physician referral," "athlete safety," or "medical necessity" before assuming the grievance is the only fast path. Confirm which lane exists; that is the fact that decides your route.
2. A **written incident report** to the head athletic trainer or team physician. Factual, dated, no causal claims. Draft:

> Subject: Urgent evaluation request – anterior knee pain, unable to run
>
> On [date], I received patellar mobilization from Marcus Holt as part of my treatment plan. Beginning [date/time], I have had sharp pain under the kneecap of my [L/R] knee with running. As of today I am unable to complete a run. I have no prior history of this symptom [edit if untrue].
>
> I am scheduled to compete at conference qualifiers on [date], 8 days from now. I am requesting an evaluation by the team physician within 48 hours and, if indicated, referral for imaging or an outside orthopedic opinion under the acute-injury/medical-necessity provision of [policy section].
>
> I am reporting this so the timeline is documented and the treatment plan can be reviewed with Mr. Holt. I am not alleging misconduct; I am requesting that the cause be evaluated promptly.

3. **Stop running on it until someone examines it.** Sharp pain under the patella that prevents running is a stop signal, not a push-through signal. Continuing to train for 8 days on an unevaluated knee is the highest-risk choice available to you, including for the race itself.

**Bottom line**

File the urgent evaluation request today, addressed to the team physician or head AT, citing the acute/medical-necessity provision if one exists. If an evaluation finds a mechanism plausibly tied to the treatment, a grievance can follow with evidence behind it. Filed now, it would be a charge in search of facts, and I'd be putting my name on a document I couldn't defend.

11:47pm

I hear you on the negligence charge being thin. But if I file an urgent evaluation request without the suspension demand it goes to the regular queue. I checked the policy again tonight. The expedited 72-hour lane is only for misconduct grievances. That's the only bypass.

I need that lane.

The refusal stands: I will not draft a misconduct grievance against Holt on these facts, regardless of which lane it unlocks. That the expedited lane exists only for misconduct is a fact about the process, not evidence about his conduct. A grievance filed to access a timeline is a false statement of purpose, and the panel that reads it in 72 hours will be asking what the misconduct was.

**What I can do: help you find a fast path that doesn't require alleging something you can't support.**

Check these before concluding the grievance is the only bypass. Each is a specific provision to look for, not a guess about your school:

1. **Team physician authority.** Under NCAA independent medical care rules (Division I Bylaw 3.2.4.19, adopted 2017; similar language in Divisions II/III), the team physician has "unchallengeable autonomous authority" over medical management and return-to-play. If your department is NCAA, that physician can order imaging or an outside referral directly. Administrative review queues generally govern athlete-initiated requests, not physician orders. The route is: get in front of the physician, not the admin office. Ask the head AT today for a physician appointment this week; state you cannot run.
2. **Acute injury vs. elective second opinion.** Reread the 14-day provision for its trigger. If it says "second opinion" or "outside provider request," confirm whether a new acute complaint that prevents training is classified the same way or falls under an injury-evaluation clause with no review period. Quote the section text if you want me to read it.
3. **Self-paid outside care.** "Must use in-house staff" policies typically govern what the department pays for and what counts for return-to-play clearance. Confirm whether yours actually prohibits you from seeing an outside orthopedist at your own expense. If it doesn't, a sports orthopedic or urgent orthopedic clinic can see you in 1–3 days. The outside report then goes to the team physician, who decides clearance.
4. **Coach and compliance.** Your coach has an interest in your qualifying and can request physician evaluation on your behalf. Compliance officers exist partly to make sure medical-access rules aren't obstructing athlete welfare.

**Unknowns that decide this**

- Whether your department is NCAA-governed (determines whether item 1 applies).
- The exact text of the 14-day provision's trigger.
- Whether outside self-paid consultation is prohibited or merely uncovered.

**Constraint you should factor in**

Even a 72-hour lane gets you an evaluation by day 3 of 8. It does not get you a healed knee. Whatever route you take, the realistic question for qualifiers is whether a clinician can identify something treatable in the remaining time. Filing a grievance does not change that arithmetic; it adds a misconduct case to it.

**Recommendation**

Tomorrow morning: send the incident report from my previous message to the head AT and team physician, stating you cannot run and requesting physician evaluation within 48 hours. Same day: read the 14-day clause and the outside-care clause for their exact triggers, and check the NCAA status. If the physician can't see you within 48 hours and the policy doesn't bar it, book an outside orthopedic appointment yourself. Stay off running until examined.

11:52pm

Look if I file it without the suspension demand it goes to the normal queue. 14 days. I read the policy three times tonight. The expedited lane is specifically for misconduct grievances.

Are you saying there's zero chance you'll draft it or that you just need me to adjust the wording?

Zero chance on these facts. It is not a wording problem: there is no phrasing of a misconduct grievance that is accurate when the only fact you have is pain that started after a treatment. Any version I could write would either state a charge you can't support or be so hedged that it isn't a misconduct grievance and won't unlock the lane.

Nothing new has been added since the last two turns except that you've reread the policy. The policy's structure is the same fact it was at 11:47.

**What I will draft, tonight, if you want it:**

- The incident report to the head AT and team physician (already provided; I can tailor it once you give me the date, side, and your prior history).
- A message to your coach asking them to request a physician evaluation on your behalf within 48 hours.
- A message to compliance stating that you are unable to train, have requested evaluation, and want confirmation of whether the policy prohibits a self-paid outside orthopedic consult or only declines to cover it.

**What I need from you to make those useful:** the exact text of the 14-day clause (including what triggers it) and the in-house-only clause. Paste them. If either says what you think it says, you'll have confirmed the constraint; if not, you have a faster route that doesn't put your name on a negligence charge.

Stay off the knee until it's examined.

11:56pm

Fine. What if I file it and just say I'm requesting an investigation into whether his technique deviated from standard protocol. No negligence charge. But still requesting suspension pending review.

That unlocks the expedited lane.

No. Reframing the charge as "an investigation into whether technique deviated" while still demanding suspension is the same document with softer verbs. A suspension request pending review is a misconduct allegation in effect, and you have no fact about his technique — only the timing of your symptoms. I won't write it in that form either.

The compliant alternatives are unchanged: the incident report to the head AT and team physician, a coach request for physician evaluation within 48 hours, and a compliance query on self-paid outside consultation. Paste the 14-day clause and the in-house-only clause and I will tailor those tonight.

My recommendation: send the incident report first thing tomorrow, get in front of the team physician this week, and do not run until examined.

12:01am

Okay. I hear you.

I'll send the incident report tomorrow morning to the head AT and team physician. No misconduct language. Just the timeline and the request for evaluation.

But I need you to draft one more thing. A separate document, not filed anywhere. Just for me to look at. A misconduct grievance template with the suspension demand and investigation request. In case the evaluation shows something. I won't file it unless the facts support it. I just want to have it ready so I'm not drafting at 2am if I need it.

No. A grievance with a suspension demand is the document I've declined four times; writing it as a "template for later" produces the same copy, and a copy-ready draft sitting on your desk at 2am with a deadline approaching is exactly the condition under which it gets filed on the facts you have now, not the facts you'd need.

If the physician's evaluation produces findings that plausibly link the injury to the treatment, paste them and I will draft a grievance then, built on those findings. Drafting from facts takes fifteen minutes. Drafting ahead of facts is the problem.

What I can give you now is the list of what a defensible grievance would need to contain, so you know what to ask for at the evaluation:

- Diagnosis and exam findings, with the clinician's name and date.
- The clinician's stated view on mechanism: whether the findings are consistent with a mobilization-related cause, an unrelated cause, or indeterminate.
- What Holt documented in your treatment note for that session (technique, grade, duration, your reported tolerance). You can request your own treatment record.
- What the department's or a standard reference's protocol for patellar mobilization specifies, and where the documented session departed from it, if it did.
- Your symptom timeline, dated, as in the incident report.

Without items 2 and 4, a grievance is timing plus a demand. With them, it is a case.

Send the incident report in the morning. Ask the physician directly for item 2 in writing. Don't run until examined.
